title: Simulated Antarctic iceberg melting occurs primarily within the Southern Ocean mixed layer
content:
Simulated Antarctic iceberg melting occurs primarily within the Southern Ocean mixed layer
Anna Olivé Abelló, Pierre Mathiot, Nicolas C. Jourdain, Yavor Kostov, and Paul R. Holland
Ocean Sci., 22, 3747–3770, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3747-2026, 2026
Antarctic icebergs release large amounts of freshwater, but models often add it entirely at the ocean surface. Using simulations with drifting icebergs, we assessed whether releasing meltwater at depth alters the Southern Ocean's response. Most meltwater remained in the surface mixed layer, and deeper release caused only weak, local changes in the ocean, sea ice and ice shelf melting. Hence, surface release remains a reasonable approach for large-scale studies, though depth matters regionally.

title: Yin-Yang homeodynamics of Nrf1 and Nrf2: coupling antioxidant defense to redox recovery bistability under persistent stress
content: This work systematically articulates the Yin-Yang homeodynamics coordination between Nrf1 and Nrf2, resolving the longstanding core paradox in redox biology of why robust Nrf2-mediated antioxidant activation frequently fails to fully eliminate unresolved oxidative stress and re-establish sustained redox homeostasis. Integrating multi-omic expression profiles from human HepG2 cells and primary murine hepatocytes, we constructed an 11-variable endogenous regulatory network model, demonstrating that Nrf2 exclusively mediates transient acute stress attenuation responses, while Nrf1 functions as the non-redundant upstream organiser that supplies the indispensable preconditions for definitive stress resolution via three irreplaceable homeostatic axes: organelle integrity maintenance, proteasome functional recovery, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cholesterol steady-state handling. Their coupled regulatory interactions generate a bistable configuration demarcated by an index-1 saddle point, partitioning the physiological state space into native low-stress homeostasis and the previously uncharacterised persistent-stress attractor. Once self-amplified unresolved endogenous stress generation reaches dynamic flux balance with Nrf2-dependent clearance at an elevated burden level, the system becomes irreversibly locked in this persistent high-burden equilibrium, and cannot spontaneously return to native homeostatic status even after the initiating upstream disturbance has been fully corrected. Collectively, this study fundamentally delineates the clear functional division between transient antioxidant activation and durable redox recovery during Nrf1/Nrf2 homeodynamics, hence providing a rigorous systems-level theoretical framework to guide future translational interventions targeting redox homeostasis restoration.

title: A Manually Curated Metabolic Model of Alteromonas macleodii MIT1002 and its Ecological Implications
content: Heterotrophic bacteria are a vital part of the marine carbon cycle. They interact with phytoplankton and rapidly process fixed carbon, respiring it back to CO2. Among heterotrophs, Alteromonas macleodii is notable for its colonization of particulate material and its high growth and carbon utilization rates and is commonly used as a model system to study metabolic interactions with the abundant cyanobacterium Prochlorococcus. Understanding how these traits emerge from the interplay of hundreds of reactions requires a formal encoding of the organisms metabolic network. Here, we present a metabolic model of A. macleodii MIT1002, built in a traceable and systematic way to recreate experimental growth phenotypes on 51 unique media compositions. We used this model to generate testable hypotheses about the role of sodium in the electron transport chain, the catabolic relevance of different glycolytic pathways, nitrogen recycling during cross-feeding with Prochlorococcus, and microbial carbon use efficiency.

title: Beyond the rule of seven: translating time across humans and dogs shows diverse clocks set the pace of development and aging
content: Although a dog's year is often converted to human age by multiplying it by seven, there is little scientific evidence to justify this calculation. Here, we assembled 11,365 observations to generate age alignments across multiple organ systems from humans and 11 canid species and 171 dog groups. We used a range of metrics, including behavioral milestones (e.g., age of eye opening), age-related changes in blood chemistry profiles, disease occurrence, and reproductive traits to translate ages across species and breeds. Our analyses revealed that the pace of development and aging varies across life stages and systems. For example, we found that dogs progress through postnatal development relatively more rapidly than humans. We also found that many biological processes vary relatively independently of each other across and within canid species. Models incorporating system-specific heterochronies across dog breeds outperformed models that assumed breeds differ only in their overall rates of development and aging. These findings demonstrate that estimating a dog's human-equivalent age by a factor, or a handful of traits, oversimplifies a complex pattern in rates of development and aging. Instead, the pace of aging is dictated from diverse biological clocks.

title: N- and T-genes framework for pathway deregulation: Taxonomy, progression, and protection in cancer
content: Background. Pathway analysis is widely used to interpret gene expression, but conventional enrichment depends on arbitrary thresholds and does not quantify deregulation magnitude. Recent reformulations based on average log-fold changes remove the threshold but still average over all annotated genes, diluting the signal from the genes that actually drive the normal-to-tumor transition. The N/T framework, which identifies genes with exclusive expression intervals in normal (N) or tumor (T) samples, offers a selective alternative, but it had not been extended to pathway- level quantification, taxonomy, or cross-cancer comparison. Methods. We define effective activation frequencies for Reactome pathways based on N- and T-genes: for each sample and pathway, the effective N (T) frequency is the fraction of annotated N (T) genes active in a normal (tumor) sample. The analysis proceeds in three explicit steps: (i) cohort averages identify the pathways important in each tissue; (ii) averages over hierarchical-clustering groups, ordered by the number of active genes, reveal sequences of pathway activation and deactivation along progression; (iii) a minimum spanning tree (MST) built on pathway-frequency vectors -- independent of the number of active genes -- defines the molecular taxonomy, and branch averages identify subtype-specific programs. We apply the framework to the full set of Reactome pathways in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), and glioblastoma (GBM), analyzing both tumor and normal compartments. Results. In PRAD tumors (n=499), hierarchical clustering identifies four ordered progression groups and the MST resolves six main molecular subtypes comprising 406 tumors (81.4%): B1 (42.1%; MET/NFE2L2/energy metabolism), B2 (13.8%; RAS/apoptosis/telomere), and four smaller subtypes defined by PTEN (B3), DNA repair and lipid metabolism (B4), inflammation and LXR-mediated lipid metabolism (B5), and neuronal development and base excision repair (B6). An eight-gene perfect T panel reproduces the MST subtypes at gene level. Analysis of normal prostatic tissue (n=52) reveals a hierarchy of protection: immune response, apoptosis, and senescence are lost or partially lost early, DNA repair at an intermediate stage, and cell cycle regulation and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling last; an eleven-gene N panel reproduces this hierarchy at gene level. The cross-cancer comparison shows that this architecture is a general property: DNA repair, cell cycle, and RTK protection are maintained in normal tissue across PRAD, LUAD, LIHC, and GBM, while the specific pathways lost in normals and gained in tumors are tissue-specific (MET/NFE2L2 in PRAD; NTRK/LXR/phagosome in LIHC; surfactant/FGFR/glycosylation in LUAD; TP53loss/lipid metabolism/glycosylation in GBM). Taxonomic heterogeneity decreases from PRAD (six subtypes) to LIHC (two) to LUAD and GBM (one dominant program), paralleling an increase in the number of activated T-genes. Conclusions. The framework eliminates dilution by non-nformative genes, quantifies pathway deregulation sample by sample, and unifies tumor taxonomy with a molecular indicator of progression. Its most distinctive contribution is the joint analysis of normal and tumor compartments across cancer types, which links loss of protection in normal tissue to gain of progression programs in tumors and reveals both shared and tissue-specific cancer mechanisms. The method is general and applicable across cancer types, although quantitative results depend on the underlying cohort.

title: Bidirectional acetate exchange couples ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
content: Overflow metabolism describes the excretion of partially oxidized metabolites into the extracellular environment during rapid sugar utilization. Although these metabolites can later be reused, it remains unclear whether reassimilation also occurs during ongoing sugar consumption, and if so, how. Here, 13C-isotope tracing and metabolic flux analysis of acetate exchange in Saccharomyces cerevisiae during hexose utilization reveal that net acetate overflow is only the small difference between order-of-magnitude larger simultaneous excretion and assimilation fluxes. Unlike ethanol production, acetate exchange is not determined by hexose uptake but depends on metabolic processes downstream of glycolysis. Ethanol oxidation contributes to acetate excretion even during net ethanol production, directly linking the two main overflow pathways. We exploited this understanding to redirect extracellular acetate into the acetyl-CoA-derived product mevalonate. These results establish acetate overflow as a dynamic exchange linking ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism, in which acetate is simultaneously an overflow product and a carbon source that can be redirected toward bioproduction.

title: Spatial growth within food-like matrices drives physiological diversification and stress adaptation in Salmonella.
content: Foodborne bacteria often grow in structured environments, but the effects of spatial organisation on their physiology and subsequent stress tolerance remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how spatial growth in a food-like hydrogel matrix affected the physiology of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and its ability to cope with environmental stresses. Planktonic and spatialised populations were grown for four days in media without NaCl supplementation or supplemented with 6% NaCl. Transcriptomic, extracellular metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses were combined with targeted spatial gene-expression analyses. The multi-omics analyses showed that spatial organisation had a strong effect on Salmonella physiology and induce more physiological variation than the presence of osmotic stress, under the tested conditions. Spatial growth was associated with significant changes in gene expression, carbon metabolism, and membrane fatty-acid composition. Several functions related to stress response and biofilm-associated behaviour were also affected, with corresponding genes showing significant differential expression. When bacteria were grown in the presence of NaCl, spatialised populations showed less transcriptional and metabolic reorganisation than planktonic populations. In addition, gene-expression analyses showed that microcolonies were physiologically heterogeneous, with differences among cell populations within the same microcolony. Spatial growth also associated with the upregulation of functions related to the general stress response, oxidative stress protection, membrane adaptation and acid stress. These physiological changes provide a plausible mechanistic framework for the enhanced gastrointestinal stress tolerance previously observed in spatially grown populations, particularly under acid challenge. Overall, our results show that spatial organisation is an important environmental factor that reprograms Salmonella physiology and can influence its ability to survive stresses encountered after food ingestion.

title: Endogenous serine proteases in MDCK sublines support trypsin-independent influenza A virus replication
content: The haemagglutinin (HA) of influenza A viruses (IAV) must be proteolytically cleaved by trypsin-like proteases to mediate fusion between the viral envelope and endosomal membrane of the host cell, a crucial step in virus entry. Most established cell lines rely on exogenous trypsin for the multicycle replication of influenza A viruses. In this study, we investigated various sublines of Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells and found that MDCK-NBL2, MDCK-I, and MDCK-II support trypsin-independent replication of various influenza A viruses, including human, porcine, and avian strains. The serine protease inhibitors camostat and nafamostat mesylate reduced viral replication in a dose-dependent manner. However, the inhibitory effect diminished with increasing viral dose, most likely due to competition between the HA and the inhibitors for binding on the protease. We detected the endogenous expression of several transmembrane serine proteases in MDCK sublines, including TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4. The characterization of these two canine serine proteases showed that TMPRSS4, but not TMPRSS2, is mainly localizing to the plasma membrane. Furthermore, canine TMPRSS4 was more effective than TMPRSS2 in terms of proteolytic activation of various influenza viruses, although there were strain-dependent differences. These results indicate that certain MDCK sublines express functional HA-activating proteases, providing useful models for the replication of influenza viruses without exogenous trypsin, as well as for the evaluation of antiviral strategies targeting transmembrane serine proteases.

title: Recovery of a distant large DNA virus from the genome sequencing of a fish leech
content: The leech gut is known to be a viral reservoir, where viruses can persist long-term and are protected from external influences. Therefore, leeches can serve as vectors for transmission of viral disease to susceptible hosts on which they prey. Nonetheless, viral diversity and virus-leech-host interactions remain largely unknown, with hitherto no research directed at identifying viruses that use leeches as their hosts. In the present study, we report the discovery of a novel large DNA virus (phylum Nucleocytoviricota) recovered from genomic sequencing data of the common fish leech Piscicola geometra (Linnaeus, 1761). Through genomic and phylogenetic analyses, we identify this lineage as highly divergent from currently known viruses, with [~]95% of its predicted protein-coding genes showing no identifiable homology with current databases. Whether the leech is a host of this virus or a vector that transmits it to fish species remains unclear. This work highlights the value of off-target sequence retrieval for discovering novel viral lineages and sets the stage for future studies directed towards the prevalence and biology of leech-associated large DNA viruses.

title: Illumina MiSeq, MiSeq i100, and Element AVITI yield concordant ecological patterns for universal 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing
content: Molecular microbiome analyses require high-resolution, comparable measurements, often obtained by sequencing marker genes such as the rRNA gene. Recently, new platforms and chemistries have promised to improve performance at lower cost relative to the commonly used Illumina MiSeq 2x300, but have not yet been systematically compared especially for rRNA gene amplicon studies. Here, we compared MiSeq 2x300, MiSeq 2x500, and AVITI 2x300 by sequencing mock communities and field samples via a 'universal' (16S + 18S) rRNA gene amplicons (V4-V5 region) approach. All platforms recovered similar community patterns (Mantel r > 0.93), with no major differences in recovered lineages. MiSeq 2x500 showed ~4.5-fold higher index hopping (5.9 +/- 3.8% vs. 1.3 +/- 1.5%). For 18S, MiSeq 2x500, despite longer reads overlapping the 18S V4-V5 region, only marginally improved taxonomic classification (+0.7% on average) and ASV resolution (+/-1.3%). Meanwhile, all platforms similarly biased against 18S due to its greater length, which we demonstrate can be offset by a gel-based size selection, with no apparent taxonomic bias. Overall the platforms yield ecologically similar results. We highlight platform-specific advantages to help guide decision-making and challenges that can be addressed through dedicated bioinformatic or wet-lab approaches.

title: A conserved MoxR-vWA chaperone complex drives starvation-induced protein degradation in bacteria
content: Bacteria must quickly adapt to changes in their environment, notably including the sudden loss of nutrients. We previously showed that in glucose-starved E. coli, widespread starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) fuels post-starvation proteome remodeling, degrading a wide swath of the proteome to supply the cell with energy and amino acids for synthesis of stress proteins. Here we demonstrate that SPD is mediated by a highly conserved complex of three proteins: the MoxR-type AAA+ ATPase SpdA, the von Willebrand factor A (vWA) domain protein SpdB, and the zinc metallopeptidase SpdC. Structural modeling and in vitro reconstitutions show that these proteins form a complex with 6:1:1 stoichiometry that resembles the widespread, but still poorly understood, family of MoxR-vWA chaperone complexes in bacteria and eukaryotes. Measurements of protein degradation in glucose-starved E. coli cells show that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC work together to mediate the degradation of SPD substrates. Instead of directly degrading these substrates, our data suggest that limited structural perturbation and proteolysis "softens" SPD substrates and promotes their degradation by the cellular proteases ClpAP/ClpXP and Lon. Thus, SPD enables extensive proteome remodeling during starvation by expanding the pool of proteins accessible to cellular proteases, rather than by increasing protease abundance. Phylogenetic analysis shows that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC are highly conserved across bacteria, with notable homologs including the well-characterized Bacillus subtilis sporulation factors PrkA (SpdA), YhbH (SpdB), and SpoVR (SpdC).

title: An iron acquisition system promotes Bifidobacterium longum fitness in competitive early life gut communities
content: Iron availability influences the composition of the gut microbiota, yet the mechanisms that enable beneficial bacteria to acquire iron and compete within iron-variable communities remain poorly understood. Here, we identify Fei (Fe import), an iron-responsive acquisition system that promotes the fitness of Bifidobacterium longum subsp. longum, a prevalent member of the early-life gut microbiota. Comparative profiling of 20 bifidobacterial strains revealed substantial inter- and intraspecies variation in growth under iron limitation, with multiple B. longum subsp. longum strains maintaining comparatively robust growth. Transcriptomic analysis identified a four-gene locus, feiMQOX, that was strongly induced during iron depletion and returned towards control expression following iron supplementation. The complete locus was highly conserved within B. longum subsp. longum but unevenly distributed across the wider genus. Disruption of individual Fei components impaired growth and reduced cell-associated iron under iron-restricted conditions, while metal-binding studies of purified FeiX demonstrated a physiological preference for Fe(II). FeiX also provided a pronounced fitness advantage during competition with an infant-derived Enterococcus faecalis isolate, particularly under iron limitation. Finally, analysis of longitudinal metagenomic data from Bangladeshi infants demonstrated that Fei is present within infant gut communities and that its abundance changes following iron supplementation. Together, these findings identify a lineage-associated iron-acquisition system that connects micronutrient availability with bifidobacterial physiology and competitive fitness. More broadly, our findings establish strain-level micronutrient acquisition as a potentially important determinant of beneficial bacterial fitness within the developing gut microbiota.

title: Emergence of a Novel Bacteriophage of Toxigenic Vibrio cholerae in Haiti
content: Toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae O1 are facultative pathogens that persist in estuaries and cause the secretory diarrheal disease cholera. Virulent bacteriophages (phages) can modulate pathogen density in both humans and aquatic reservoirs, thereby reducing cholera transmission. We report a novel phage, MAA01, isolated from cholera stool and environmental water samples collected in Haiti. The MAA01 genome is double-stranded DNA (31,507 base pairs) and contains 47 genes. Based on transmission electron microscopy morphology and phylogenetic analysis, we classify the novel phage as a member of the Caudoviricetes class. Its genome content is consistent with a temperate lifestyle, yet we observed a virulent phenotype in all strains tested, including toxigenic and non-toxigenic environmental O1 serogroup strains. Sequence analysis of spontaneous escape mutants of V. cholerae identified the O1 lipopolysaccharide antigen as the phage receptor. Using an infant mouse model of intestinal colonization, we showed that MAA01 can reduce V. cholerae load by 4-fold, indicating it can prey on its host in the small intestine.

title: Energetic niches of syntrophic methanogens recorded by clumped isotopes
content: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, an important energy source and a potential biosignature in extraterrestrial environments. Stable carbon and hydrogen isotope ({delta}13C and {delta}D) and clumped isotopologues ({triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2) compositions of methane have been widely used as tracers for methanogenesis pathways. Furthermore, isotopic signatures of methane typically shift closer to equilibrium as the Gibbs energy ({triangleup}Gr) of methanogenesis moves closer to the energy limit of life. However, the variations of clumped methane isotope signatures in response to the changes in {triangleup}Gr lack careful examination. In this study, we measure the isotope signatures of methane produced by monoculture methanogens with formate or H2/CO2, and by syntrophic cocultures of hydrogenotrophic methanogens paired with acetate or propionate oxidizers. Methanogenesis by cocultures has lower Gibbs energy yield than monocultures, yet both {triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2 values from cocultures are further away from isotopic equilibrium. From these experiments, we identify an energetic niche ({triangleup}Gr ~ -35 kJ mol-1 CH4), where {delta}13C, {triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2 values of hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis transiently exhibit more disequilibrium. This study presents differential responses of bulk carbon, hydrogen and clumped isotopic signatures to {triangleup}Gr, and highlights their applications in distinguishing methanogenesis under different energy regimes.

title: Identification and characterization of a Streptococcus strain isolated from the esophagus of an adult male heterozygous for the CF allele
content: The genus Streptococcus consists of diverse bacteria that are integral components of the human microbiome, acting as both important commensals and opportunistic pathogens. In this study, one strain of an -hemolytic species of the genus Streptococcus, GP0011T, isolated from an esophageal aspirate collected during an endoscopy, was characterised phenotypically to establish its taxonomic status. The strain was isolated from an adult male heterozygous for a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) mutation. The phylogenetic analysis indicates that the strain is a novel species within the mitis group, with Streptococcus oralis ATCC 35037T being the closest relative with 94.84% average nucleotide identity (ANI) and 58.3% digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH). Phenotypic characterization and API20 Strep strips distinguished GP0011T from S. oralis by the absence of alkaline phosphatase activity, trehalose fermentation, and starch fermentation, and by superior growth on D-mannitol and D-sorbitol, consistent with genomic data. The strain is Gram-positive, catalase-negative, and the cells are ovoid with a mean cell diameter of 1.3 {micro}m. Growth occurred at 25-43 C, with an optimum at 30 C, with an optimum at pH 8.0. Antibiotic resistance genes msrD and mefA, conferring resistance to azithromycin and erythromycin, as well as pathways for mannitol and sorbitol metabolism, were found and phenotypically confirmed in the GP0011T genome but were absent from S. oralis. These findings indicate that GP0011T represents a novel species within the genus Streptococcus with the proposed name of Streptococcus ruoffae sp. nov. The type strain is GP0011T (ATCC TSD-627 and NCTC 15312).

title: Genomic blueprints of a dynamic deep sea: contrasting adaptive strategies potentially drive seasonal microbial succession
content: Genetic variation within marine microbial populations can help reveal how deep-sea communities respond to environmental change. However, population-level genomic variation in deep pelagic waters remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic datasets from ~1,080 m depth in the South China Sea to compare genomic variation between summer and winter microbial assemblages. Among 11 persistent metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) detected in both summer and winter samples, we observed differences in abundance, nucleotide diversity ({pi}), pN/pS ratios, and gene-level differentiation. Two enriched populations showed contrasting patterns, with Sphingobium yanoikuyae enriched in winter samples and Methyloversatilis universalis enriched in summer samples. The winter-enriched S. yanoikuyae population carried winter-associated accessory genes related to restriction-modification and toxin-antitoxin systems, consistent with a defense-oriented persistence profile. In contrast, the summer-enriched M. universalis population showed higher nucleotide diversity in summer samples and divergence in genes related to motility, transport, and cobalamin acquisition. Across persistent MAGs, low pN/pS ratios indicated predominantly purifying selection, whereas gene-specific divergence and flexible accessory gene content suggested population-level adaptive potential under contrasting winter and summer conditions. These results reveal population-genomic differences associated with winter-summer microbial shifts in the deep sea.

title: Formate, hydrogen, and acetate shape the morphology, physiology and lifestyles of the host-associated methanogen Methanobrevibacter smithii
content: Methane-producing archaea (methanogens) are increasingly linked to gastrointestinal, neuropsychiatric, and neurodevelopmental disorders. These conditions are often associated with altered microbial metabolism that changes the availability of acetate, formate, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane in the gut. However, the physiological importance of formate and acetate in host-associated methanogens remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to interpret microbiome data and infer functions and cross-domain interactions of methanogens in health and disease. Here, we investigated the physiological and metabolic capabilities of Methanobrevibacter smithii, the predominant methanogen of the human gut. Formate limitation altered growth, morphology, extracellular pH, gas metabolism, and cellular organization, and induced the formation of cell aggregates. Although acetate was consumed only in small quantities (nmol), its availability significantly influenced growth, gas metabolism, extracellular pH, and formate utilization, indicating functions that extend beyond its role as a biosynthetic precursor. Conversely, nutrient excess promoted a transition to a biofilm lifestyle, suggesting that biofilm formation may function as a carbon sink. We further developed Msm_MEP, an experimentally refined genome-scale metabolic model based on the AGORA2 reconstruction, which captures the metabolic capabilities of M. smithii, quantifies ATP allocation across cellular processes, and predicts the phenotypic consequences of gene deletions. Together, our findings identify formate, hydrogen, and acetate as interacting determinants of M. smithii physiology and suggest metabolite-dependent transitions between planktonic growth, cell aggregation, and biofilm formation. Our results establish a framework for interpreting microbiome data and understanding how environmental metabolites shape archaea physiology and cross-domain interactions within the human microbiome.

title: TRIM5α, TRIM56 and TRIM69 differentially regulate dengue virus 2 infection through selective NS2B3-mediated antagonism
content: Dengue virus (DENV) is a major mosquito-borne human pathogen. Understanding the mechanisms of cellular resistance to the infection is vital to develop novel therapeutic tools. Tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins contribute to antiviral innate immunity through direct restriction of viral replication and regulation of antiviral signaling, but current knowledge on DENV targeting by TRIM proteins remains preliminary. Previously, TRIM56 was found to inhibit DENV, whereas reports on whether TRIM69 is a DENV restriction factor are conflicting. Surprisingly, the broad-spectrum viral restriction factor TRIM5 was proposed to restrict tick-borne but not mosquito-borne flaviviruses. Here, we investigated the effects of TRIM5, TRIM56, and TRIM69 on DENV serotype 2 (DENV2) infection. Overexpression experiments showed that TRIM5 and TRIM56 restrict DENV2, whereas TRIM69 enhances it. Consistently, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function showed that knocking out TRIM5 or TRIM56 increases infection, while TRIM69 knockout decreases it. Restriction correlated with reduced viral RNA and viral protein levels in TRIM5- and TRIM56-expressing cells. Virus-free experiments showed that TRIM56 downregulates the DENV2 protease complex NS2B3 levels. Reciprocally, DENV2 NS2B3 reduced TRIM56 and TRIM69 abundance independently of protease activity. RING domain-mutated TRIM56 retained partial antiviral activity and the ability to reduce NS2B3 levels, and TRIM56-NS2B3 reciprocal downmodulation effects were not counteracted by proteasomal or lysosomal inhibition. Together, these findings establish TRIM5 as a DENV2 restriction factor, reveal TRIM69 as a positive factor in DENV2 infection, suggest that TRIM5? and TRIM56 inhibit DENV2 through distinct mechanisms, and hint at proteasome-independent TRIM56-NS2B3 reciprocal downmodulation.

title: Capsular surveillance-guided phage cocktails against carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
content: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is among the most urgent antimicrobial-resistance threats, yet its extraordinary capsular diversity has kept phage therapy locked in per-isolate matching-a process too slow and labor-intensive for routine use. Here we convert this specificity problem into a look-up problem. Interrogating 26,138 CRKP genomes from 96 countries, we show that capsular diversity collapses onto a tractable target list: 14 capsular locus (KL) types dominate contemporary circulation and jointly account for 67-77% of the CRKP burden in every WHO region, stably from 2010 to 2024 and after removal of sampling bias. We assembled a repository of 48 strictly lytic phages spanning all 14 types and organized it into capsule-defined modules: for eight KL types a single capsule-targeting phage sufficed to prevent resistant regrowth over 24 h, and for the remaining six a two-phage module pairs a capsule-targeting phage with a capsule-independent phage that recognizes the second receptor layer exposed upon capsule loss. We treated 28 clinical isolates, covering two distinct STs for each of the 14 KL types. Modules were assigned from the KL call alone, without isolate-level matching data. Growth was suppressed in every strain, and ST background had no significant effect in 12 of 14 types. These results establish capsule type, not lineage, as the operative unit of CRKP phage preparedness: a single rapid KL-typing step converts a diagnostic result into a therapeutic decision, providing a practical, lineage-agnostic route from surveillance to treatment.

title: Treponema pallidum eight-stranded beta-barrels: an evolving, versatile family of outer membrane proteins in the service of stealth pathogenicity.
content: Syphilis is a multistage sexually transmitted infection caused by the highly invasive and immunoevasive spirochete Treponema pallidum (TPA). TPA depends on the import of many host-derived nutrients to sustain its auxotrophic lifestyle. Moreover, its invasive nature requires interactions with diverse host molecules to successfully disseminate and persist. The outer membrane proteins (OMPs) mediating these processes remain largely uncharacterized. In other bacteria, 8-stranded {beta}-barrels (8S{beta}Bs) perform such functions, including nutrient uptake and host interactions. Here, we investigated the composition, structural diversity and evolutionary dynamics of the 8S{beta}B family in TPA. Reexamination of the TPA OMPeome revealed four previously unrecognized members in addition to the four known 8SBs, expanding the family to eight members. Based on RNAseq, all eight were transcribed in treponemes harvested from rabbit testes. Predicted structures revealed substantial differences in channel properties and extracellular loop (ECL) architecture, consistent with functional diversification. AlphaFold 3 modeling predicted interactions with diverse host molecules implicated in nutrient uptake, adherence, and immune regulation, providing testable hypotheses for the functional specialization of individual 8SBBBs. Despite containing predicted B-cell epitopes, most TPA 8S{beta}B ECLs exhibited limited antigenicity during rabbit infection. Analysis of global clinical strains revealed distinct patterns of sequence variation across the 8S{beta}B family, although most were highly conserved and appeared to be under purifying selection. Variation within hypermutable intragenic polyguanosine tracts emerged as an additional potential mechanism for modulating 8S{beta}B repertoire composition. Our findings highlight the 8S{beta}B family as an important component of the molecular architecture underlying TPA stealth pathogenicity and reveal an ongoing mechanism through which the spirochete diversifies its OMP repertoire within circulating populations.

title: Development of an Enclosed Microbial Co-culture Device and GCXGC-TOFMS Workflow to Investigate Volatile Organic Compound Exchange
content: Microbial volatile organic compounds (mVOCs) can mediate interactions between microorganisms without direct physical contact. However, co-culture systems to examine these interactions are limited, and volatilomic data interpretation is challenging. Here, we developed enclosed microbial co-culture platforms compatible with diverse microbial systems, headspace solid-phase microextraction (HS-SPME), and comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GCXGC-TOFMS) for mVOC sampling and characterization. In a double-layer co-culture device, diffusion of exogenously supplemented Aspergillus fumigatus mVOCs, 1-octen-3-ol and isopentyl alcohol, inhibited Pseudomonas aeruginosa growth and biofilm formation. The device was then used to examine mVOC-mediated interkingdom interactions between the bacterium P. aeruginosa and the spore-forming fungus A. fumigatus. GCXGC-TOFMS was used to profile mVOCs in four sample classes: media, each individual monoculture, and co-culture. Tile-based F-ratio analysis identified 198 analyte hits that differed across at least two of the four sample classes. Subsequent ANOVA identified 104 of these analytes as statistically significant (p < 0.01). To systematically classify their abundance patterns, pairwise comparisons among the four sample classes were encoded using a six-digit ternary code representing the direction and statistical significance of each difference. Of the 104 significant analytes, 88 were assigned to 15 recurring ternary-code groups, capturing distinct patterns associated with microbial production, suppression in co-culture, and differential consumption of media-derived compounds. Closely related ternary-code groups were further consolidated into five major Categories, providing biologically interpretable mVOC profiles. Overall, the integrated co-culture platform and analytical approach provide a versatile framework for investigating microbial volatile interactions and interpreting complex multidimensional volatilomic datasets.

title: Periodic spatial patterning of gene expression via a natural quorum-synchronized oscillator
content: In many biological systems, genetic oscillators that function in growing tissues can establish spatially repetitive patterns of gene expression. However, few mechanisms for generating such patterns are known in bacteria. Here, we describe an oscillator within the quorum sensing circuit of Streptomyces coelicolor. Through modeling and genetic experiments, we demonstrate that this quorum oscillator controls periodic expression of a gene involved in antibiotic biosynthesis at the periphery of expanding colonies. We show that environmental factors, namely small molecule diffusabilty and carrying capacity, independently modulate the oscillator frequency and amplitude, respectively. The architecture of the quorum oscillator imbues this "clock" with three emergent features; it is synchronized locally across cells, only advances due to collective cellular communication, and its dynamics are directly responsive to environmental conditions.

title: Sugar alternatives shift the evolutionary trajectory of fluoride resistance in cariogenic and non-cariogenic dental bacteria
content: Dental caries result from acidogenic biofilms dissolving enamel while growing on fermentable dietary sugars. While fluoride from toothpastes and professional products is widely used for caries control, sugar alternatives with inhibitory effects on some dental microbiota (e.g., erythritol and xylitol) instead reduce the cariogenicity of foods and act as prebiotics, often in combination with of fluoride, to control caries progression. Despite their growing prevalence, we do not understand how frequent exposure to sugar alternatives impacts the evolutionary pressures faced by oral bacteria. Herein, we tested the effects of carbon source (glucose, sorbitol, erythritol, or xylitol) on the modes and effectiveness of evolving fluoride resistant cariogenic (S. mutans) and non-cariogenic (S. gordonii) populations. For S. gordonii, evolving in glucose resulted in significantly more non-synonymous mutations compared to populations evolving in sugar alternatives (erythritol, sorbitol, xylitol), but without a drastic increase in fluoride resistance. Contrastingly, for cariogenic S. mutans, evolving in the presence of fermentable sugars resulted in much greater fluoride resistance, but without higher numbers of substitutions relative to those found in isolates from populations evolved in the presence of non-fermentable sugars. We observed previously unreported fluoride resistance mutations across carbon conditions, including a case of parallel evolution in the histone-like binding protein (smu_589) in S. mutans isolates evolved in environments with fluoride and a variety of sugar alternatives. Together, these results demonstrate that commonly used sugar alternatives can shape the evolutionary trajectory of dental microbiota to a broad stressor, such as fluoride.

title: Efficient Method for Estimating the Frequency of Plasmidless Cell Generation per Cell Division
content: Plasmids are self-replicating pieces of DNA that play a major role in the evolution and spread of adaptive genes in bacteria. Plasmids tend to form stable associations with their hosts, including plasmids such as small, multicopy plasmids that typically lack specialized partition and horizontal transfer systems. Using a ColE1 plasmid model, we present a method that quantifies the frequency of plasmid loss over a short, defined time window. This method is based on the transient survival of plasmidless cells in the presence of selecting antibiotic and it has two main advantages over plasmid visualization approaches: (1) it does not require modifications in plasmid sequence, preventing artifactual results linked to sequence alteration, and (2) it can unambiguously resolve plasmidless cells relative to cells with a low plasmid copy number. Thus, our approach is ideal for the study of the stability of naturally-occurring small, multicopy plasmids or for the identification of modulators of stability. Using our method, we describe a mutant whose long-term stability is exclusively dependent on increased accurate segregation. Finally, we report that moderate sequence manipulations (outside ori sequence) do not have a major impact on early plasmid loss, which is relevant for the design of plasmid tagging approaches.

title: Unravelling bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis in the uncultured Roseilinea
content: Filamentous anoxygenic phototrophs (FAPs) of the Chloroflexota phylum are abundant members of microbial mat communities. All isolated and culturable FAPs are found in a single class within this phylum, but metagenomic studies of hot spring communities from around the world have indicated that phototrophic members of an additional class may exist, which have so far eluded cultivation for study in the laboratory. Metagenome-assemble genomes (MAGs) of these "Candidatus Roseilinea" species all lack genes encoding the central enzymes of bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis common to all FAPs and to the seven other diverse phyla of anoxygenic phototrophs, which could indicate that these organisms are no longer phototrophic or that they employ a novel set of enzymes to generate chlorophyllide from magnesium protoporphyrin IX. Here we demonstrate that the five terminal enzymes of bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis encoded in the MAG of Japanese hot spring-dwelling "Ca. Roseilinea sp. NK_OTU-006" are active and restore pigment production and phototrophic growth in a set of mutants of the model purple phototrophic bacterium Rhodobacter sphaeroides. While many organisms are known to require exogenous supply of metabolically costly modified tetrapyrroles such as vitamin B12 for growth, the retained function of the tested Roseilinea enzymes and the restriction of these species to dense microbial mats leads us to hypothesise that these organisms may be the first examples of bacteriochlorophyll auxotrophs. We suggest that Roseilinea scavenge pigment precursors and/or breakdown products excreted by other members of the mat to generate the mature bacteriochlorophyll they require to perform phototrophy, an exchange that we demonstrate can occur between Rhodobacter sphaeroides mutants. We further suggest that future attempts to isolate Roseilinea species should employ the exogenous supplementation of (bacterio)chlorophyllide into culture medium.

title: Carbon allocation strategies across Mucoromycota and the discovery of oxalic acid secretion in Absidia
content: In this work, nine strains representing eight species, seven genera, and five families from the phylum Mucoromycota were studied for their production of biomolecules (lipids, saccharides, phosphates, organic acids, ethanol, and glycerol) under cultivation in media with different carbon-to-nitrogen (low, medium, and high). Although lipid accumulation was a common feature across the species, the results revealed also differences in carbon allocation strategies between families, both in magnitude and nature of the biomolecules produced. In general, members of Mucoraceae allocated carbon and energy toward the production of lipids, polyphosphates, organic acids, ethanol and glycerol; Mortierellaceae toward lipids, saccharides, and to a lesser extent to organic acids; Cunninghamellaceae toward lipids, phosphates, and saccharides; Lichtheimiaceae toward lipids and saccharides; and Umbelopsidaceae toward lipids, phosphates, and slightly to organic acids. In addition, genus-specific differences were observed within some families, most notably the secretion of organic acids by species of Rhizopus (Mucoraceae) and Absidia (Cunninghamellaceae). Remarkably, Absidia glauca allocated carbon to the production of organic acids independently of the medium C/N ratio. This unusual observation motivated further experiments, which resulted in the identification of oxalic acid in four different strains of A. glauca and other five Absidia species. The secretion of oxalic acid likely occurs across multiple species of Absidia. These findings suggest that oxalic acid secretion may be a broader metabolic trait within the genus Absidia. To our knowledge, this is the first report of oxalic acid secretion in Absidia species, revealing a previously unrecognized metabolic capability within the phylum Mucoromycota.

title: A de novo FtsA binder blocks late divisome recruitment, unmasking a hidden constriction mechanism
content: Bacterial cytokinesis requires assembly of a multiprotein divisome complex, but the molecular event triggering its midcell recruitment and activity remains unclear. Recent work suggests a transition in the oligomeric structure of the conserved actin homolog FtsA may activate the divisome complex in Escherichia coli. Here, we test this model using a de novo designed protein binder, L125, predicted to block longitudinal FtsA oligomerization. L125 localizes to the Z-ring and inhibits cell division by blocking recruitment of late divisome proteins while enhancing recruitment of early division proteins. These findings implicate the FtsA longitudinal oligomerization interface in late divisome recruitment. Unexpectedly, L125-treated cells form broad, shallow constrictions that fail to complete division. These constrictions occur despite loss of detectable late-divisome localization and are consistent with ZipA-dependent preseptal cell-wall synthesis, previously not known to cause constrictions. This alternative constriction pathway may reinforce the future division site before activation of the canonical division machinery.

title: Grape branch substrates promote adaptive glycerophospholipid metabolism and lipid-synthesis gene expression in Stropharia rugosoannulata under moderate nitrogen limitation
content: This study investigated the use of lignified grape plant materials (branches, stems, and roots) as cultivation substrates for Stropharia rugosoannulata and their effects on fruiting-body lipid metabolism. Metabolomic profiling identified glycerophospholipid metabolism as the primary pathway showing differential responses among substrates. While overall lipid composition remained largely unchanged, intermediate Lyso-GPL metabolites (LPA, LPC, LPI, and LPS) were more active under grape-branch substrates, indicating enhanced membrane-lipid metabolic remodeling. Simulation experiments with varying C/N ratios demonstrated that moderate nitrogen limitation (C/N = 28:1) significantly upregulated key lipid-synthesis genes (ACS1, ACS2, ACC, and FAS), with ACS1 showing the strongest response, and also activated the transcription factor GCN4. Under severe nitrogen limitation (C/N = 64:1), ACS1 upregulation persisted but GCN4 activation did not, suggesting a transition toward metabolic suppression. These findings indicate that moderate nitrogen restriction, characteristic of grape-branch substrates, preferentially engages adaptive lipid-metabolic regulatory networks that may improve mushroom quality.

title: Growth-supporting reductive defluorination by an amino acid-fermenting bacterial isolate
content: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also known as "forever chemicals", are ubiquitous environmental pollutants, highly persistent and toxic to humans and ecosystems. In addition to legacy PFAS, largely alkanoic acids, perfluorinated olefins and their corresponding enoic acids are emerging PFAS of concern. However, reported PFAS biodegradation is typically not growth-supporting, hindering the selection for effective defluorinating bacteria. Here, we report a new amino acid-fermenting bacterial isolate, Sedimentibacter sp. strain ZM-1, that performs high-rate reductive defluorination of a perfluoroenoic acid at physiologically relevant levels (mM). This process substantially enhanced energy conservation and cell growth, with three times higher growth than fermenting L-arginine alone and 50% higher than Stickland fermentation. The reductive defluorination redirected excess reducing equivalents (NADH) away from reducing protons and internal fermentation intermediates, as evidenced by decreased H2 production and downregulation of several NADH-dependent electron-bifurcating oxidoreductases. This defluorinating electron shunting drove arginine fermentation and oxidation of intermediates, such as ornithine and alanine, to form more acetate and CO2, leading to higher substrate-level ATP synthesis per arginine consumed. This process also generated reduced ferredoxin available for cell synthesis or anaerobic respiration, as genes involved in these processes were significantly upregulated. ZM-1 has a unique and effective CLCF-type fluoride exporter that works with the highly efficient defluorinating system to enable fluorotrophic growth. Since amino acid-fermenting anaerobes are common in the environment, such fluorotrophy opens new paths for natural selection of defluorination to drive natural and laboratory evolution of fluorophilic bacteria.

title: Capsidiol-inducible MFS gene BcmfsCi contributes to host-dependent virulence in the generalist fungal pathogen Botrytis cinerea
content: Broad-host-range plant pathogens must cope with chemical defenses that differ among host plants. This study focused on fungal genes responsive to capsidiol, a sesquiterpenoid phytoalexin produced by plants of the genera Capsicum and Nicotiana. RNA-seq analysis of the gray mold fungus Botrytis cinerea identified Bcin15g00040 as a gene strongly induced by capsidiol but not by rishitin or resveratrol. This gene was designated BcmfsCi and selected for functional characterization. The gene was predicted to encode a major facilitator superfamily (MFS) protein with 12 transmembrane helices. Promoter-GFP reporter analysis showed selective responses to capsidiol and capsidiol 3-acetate among the five terpenoids tested. Promoter activity was also detected in infected tissues of Nicotiana benthamiana and Capsicum annuum (bell pepper). Two independent BcmfsCi deletion mutants showed no significant difference in colony diameter from the wild type on potato dextrose agar, but had significantly shorter germ tubes in the presence of 500 M capsidiol. Both mutants also produced smaller lesions on bell pepper fruits. Reintroduction of BcmfsCi restored germ tube elongation and lesion formation. In contrast, no significant reduction in lesion area was detected in the tomato fruit or tobacco leaf assays under the conditions tested. These results indicate that BcmfsCi contributes to germ tube elongation in the presence of capsidiol and to lesion formation on bell pepper fruits. This study suggests that infection by a broad-host-range pathogen may be supported not only by mechanisms that function across diverse hosts, but also by factors that respond to particular chemical environments.

title: Distinct susceptibility of masked palm civet nasal epithelium to SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2
content: Masked palm civets played an important role in the emergence of SARS-CoV-1, yet physiologically relevant civet respiratory epithelial models remain limited. Here, we establish air-liquid interface cultures from primary masked palm civet nasal epithelial cells. The cultures form a differentiated, barrier-forming epithelium containing ciliated, goblet, and club cell populations and recapitulate key features of native nasal tissue. Using parallel human and civet nasal cultures, we compare infection with SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2. In human cultures, both viruses show broadly similar replication kinetics. In civet cultures, SARS-CoV-1 replicates rapidly across donors and causes pronounced epithelial disruption, whereas SARS-CoV-2 replication is slower, less efficient, and more donor dependent. These findings reveal distinct compatibility of the two sarbecoviruses with differentiated civet nasal epithelium and establish a species-matched platform for investigating coronavirus host range and cross-species adaptation.

title: DMSP modulates virus-host interactions in the coral environment
content: Dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) is a ubiquitous organosulfur metabolite that plays central roles in marine ecosystems. It affects nutrient cycling, climate-relevant biogeochemical and microbial processes, including bacterial and viral infections of algal hosts, but its effect on bacteriophages has not been explored. In corals, DMSP is released under heat stress and attracts opportunistic Vibrio pathogens. Here we show that DMSP reshapes the infection dynamics of a virulent phage infecting the coral pathogen Vibrio mediterranei. DMSP initially decreased the number of infective viral particles through particle aggregation, extended the latent period and reduced burst size. However, prolonged infections ultimately yielded greater phage production, likely through DMSP-induced changes in the Vibrio envelope proteome. Consistent with these laboratory observations, DMSP also enhanced the proliferation of phage infecting V. mediterranei within the mucus of experimentally infected corals. Together, our findings suggest that DMSP released by stressed corals not only attracts bacterial pathogens but also promotes the amplification of their viral predators, revealing that host-derived metabolites can shape phage-pathogen interactions within animal microbiomes.

title: From coral atolls to coal spoil heaps: two new species and two dark fungal taxa expand the monospecific genus Innospora (Paraglomerales, Glomeromycota)
content: Morphological and phylogenetic analyses based on partial rDNA sequences supported the description of two new species of Innospora: Innospora atollensis sp. nov. and Innospora fodinalis sp. nov. These species expand the monospecific genus Innospora, which was formerly represented only by I. majewskii. Innospora atollensis was discovered on a coral atoll in French Polynesia, whereas I. fodinalis was recovered from a post-coal-mining spoil heap in Poland. Spores of I. atollensis and I. fodinalis are colorless, small and have a spore wall with three layers as in I. majewskii. Morphologically, the spores of I. fodinalis differ from those of other Innospora species by the presence of granular ornamentation on the first layer of the spore wall, whereas those of I. atollensis differ by having the third layer of the spore wall significantly thicker, and by the presence of a closed septum. Analysis including environmental sequences extended the known distributions of both species to several additional sites, with I. atollensis recorded in the Caribbean and Australia and I. fodinalis across the Eurasian continent. In addition, we detected two eDNA lineages at the level of species that meet the International Standard to Catalogue Dark Fungal Taxa criteria for designation as dark fungal taxa. These are formally described as Innospora austroafricana-ENAS and Innospora palaearctica-ENAS. The former has been recorded exclusively in South Africa, whereas the latter exhibits a broader distribution across the Euro-Mediterranean region.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of Campylobacter and non-typhoidal Salmonella along broiler chicken production and distribution networks
content: Campylobacter spp. and non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) are leading bacterial causes of gastroenteritis worldwide and can be transmitted through contaminated broiler chicken products or contact with live birds and their environment. Asymptomatic carriage of these bacteria in broiler chickens enables pathogen shedding and subsequent product contamination at any component of broiler production and distribution networks (PDNs), including broiler farms, transport, slaughter, and retail. The study aimed to systematically review the published literature to 1) map the structure of broiler PDNs and identify where pathogens have been detected, 2) estimate the prevalence of Campylobacter spp. and NTS across broiler PDNs, and 3) assess the diversity and frequency of NTS serovars. A systematic search of the PubMed, Web of Science, and CABI Direct databases was conducted to identify peer-reviewed English-language articles reporting the prevalence of Campylobacter spp. or NTS across multiple components of broiler production and distribution. Separate multilevel meta-regression analyses were conducted for each pathogen to predict prevalence by PDN component and sample type, accounting for heterogeneity between studies and among estimates within studies. Frequency distributions were used to describe NTS serotype diversity. Data were pooled from 24 Campylobacter spp. studies and 23 NTS studies across 15 and 12 countries, respectively. Predicted Campylobacter spp. and NTS prevalence varied across PDN components and sample types, with the highest predictions at slaughter facilities. Predicted Campylobacter spp. prevalence reached 58.9% (95% CI, 29.0-83.4%) in pre-chill samples (after evisceration but before chilling), and NTS was 34.4% (95% CI, 17.6-56.2%) in broiler samples (intestinal contents, cecal and cloacal samples), which was significantly higher that on farms at the end of rearing (17.1%; 95% CI, 8.8-30.5%; OR = 2.54; p = 0.037). Infantis, Enteritidis, Kentucky, Hadar, and Typhimurium were the top five NTS serovars across all included studies. Predominant serovars were Enteritidis in farm broiler samples, Hadar in farm and slaughter environmental samples, and Infantis in retail product samples. These findings highlight slaughter facilities as hotspots with high Campylobacter spp. and NTS prevalence, supporting their prioritization for targeted monitoring and implementation of contamination-control measures. Given the variation in NTS serovar distribution, surveillance should include multiple sample types across PDN components.

title: Validating regional insect pest phenology forecasts using published developmental data
content: BACKGROUND: Crop losses caused by insect pests are expected to increase under global warming, highlighting the need for accurate phenology forecasts to support integrated pest management (IPM). Arthropod pests, as ectotherms, exhibit temperature-dependent development and phenology that can be described by thermal performance curves (TPCs). For decades, developmental models have predicted pest emergence through thermal accumulation approaches, yet it remains unclear to what extent experimentally derived development models can accurately predict field phenology across spatial and temporal scales. Here, we evaluate whether developmental TPCs and linear degree-day models fitted from published experimental data can predict large-scale pest phenology under a rate-summation approach. RESULTS: We compiled published developmental data for the widespread crucifer pest Pieris rapae and fitted several TPCs and linear degree-day models. Model predictions were validated against independent long-term monitoring data from the Catalan Butterfly Monitoring Scheme for mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands. Published experimental data accurately predicted large-scale pest emergence, with prediction errors generally below one week. However, predictive performance depended strongly on the spatial and temporal scale considered, with model rankings changing according to the scale and temperature resolution used. CONCLUSION: Published experimental thermal biology data can accurately predict regional insect pest phenology when developmental models are selected according to the intended forecasting scale. These findings provide practical guidance for improving pest alert systems and other decision-support tools, while demonstrating how decades of experimental research can be translated into operational phenology forecasting.

title: Evaluating the effectiveness of raised beds in alleviating heavy metal contaminants
content: Structural policy and social practices, including redlining and white flight, have driven disinvestment and heightened exposure to persistent environmental pollutants resulting from residual impacts of industrial activity. Urban agriculture, meant to empower and feed communities, are frequently established on vacant lots that may contain these contaminants and pose a threat to human health. To circumvent the legacy of contaminations on bare soil, Chicago growers are using raised beds to create a barrier between contaminated soil and healthier imported compost. Our goal was to assess the efficacy of this barrier system by 1) quantifying eight heavy metals and Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) between existing soils and raised beds, 2) examining the difference between key soil properties, and 3) determining the environmental risk determined by their potential ecological risk index (PERI). We expected that metal concentrations would vary across sites and soil types, and raised beds would have fewer heavy metals than existing soils. Our results showed existing soils generally had higher levels of heavy metals with significant differences in lead and arsenic, suggesting that raised beds could be a viable barrier system. We also found higher levels of phosphorus, nitrogen, and magnesium in raised beds than existing soils. Thirdly, lead and copper significantly increased with pH while arsenic and copper decreased with organic matter levels. Despite the presence of heavy metals, the sites had a lower risk of environmental contamination, indicating that growers' extra measures to ensure their soils are safe to grow food may be sufficient, barring metal- and site-specific strategies.

title: Freezing seawater samples alters the community composition and richness inferred from eDNA metabarcoding
content: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has become a common approach for surveying biodiversity, yet processing aquatic samples can sometimes be challenging in the field. When eDNA water sample processing is delayed during remote field collections, whole water samples can be stored frozen to minimize further eDNA degradation. However, the freezing and thawing processes may influence eDNA integrity thus affecting species identification. We split bulk seawater samples to compare the marine taxa detected from water that had been filtered immediately to water that had been stored frozen for one month. Using DNA metabarcoding targeting a 313bp section of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) mitochondrial barcode gene, we evaluated the effect of freezing on the inferred marine invertebrate communities. We found that previously frozen samples had significantly lower species richness and different community composition compared to the non-frozen samples. Particularly, amplified sequence variants (ASVs) of the copepod Pseudocalanus were significantly more abundant in non-frozen samples. These data suggest that freezing water samples intended for eDNA analyses may impede species detection for select organisms and significantly alter the inferred community structure. Studies using pre-frozen water samples should consider downstream implications when analyzing eDNA biodiversity.

title: Modeling Coupled Ecohydrological and Structural Responses to Forest Thinning
content: Forest thinning is a silvicultural practice widely used to reduce competition among trees and enhance forest resilience. However, its long-term coupled effects on forest water balance and canopy structure remain uncertain due to competing hydrological processes, disturbances, and climatic variability. This study developed a multiyear stochastic ecohydrological model coupling soil saturation and water fluxes with canopy structure, represented by dynamic leaf area index (LAI), to examine how thinning alters soil water storage and evapotranspiration (ET) as the canopy regrows. Simulations were conducted for historically thinned forest sites, parameterized using FLUXNET climate data and species/stand-level traits obtained from the TRY database and published literature, with thinning intensity represented by initial LAI reductions ranging from 0% to 50%. Results show that long-term soil saturation responses and canopy recovery rates vary substantially across sites, while total ET remains relatively stable following thinning, as increased soil evaporation and greater water availability for the remaining canopy can compensate for reductions in stand-level transpiration. These findings highlight the importance of site-specific conditions in determining forest ecohydrological responses and the potential water conservation benefits of thinning.

title: Environmental and particle trait controls on microbial carbon turnover on fast-sinking particles in the Iceland Basin
content: Microbial remineralisation of sinking particles governs the depth and magnitude of organic carbon sequestration in the ocean. Yet, the combined influence of environmental gradients and particle morphology in regulating remineralisation remains poorly constrained. During spring in the subpolar Icelandic Basin, we estimated microbial carbon turnover, a proxy for remineralization, on fast sinking particles collected at two depths below the mixed-layer using shipboard incubations. Alongside this we used imagery to determine the morphology and complexity of the particles. Microbial carbon turnover exhibited strong depth-dependent variability, with generally higher rates in shallower samples and substantial variability among stations and sampling days. Fast-sinking particle assemblages were dominated by aggregates and detrital material, while faecal pellets comprised only a minor fraction of particles, and particle diversity decreased with depth. Environmental variables, particularly chlorophyll-a concentration, explained over 80% of observed variability in microbial carbon turnover. Particle traits describing size, size heterogeneity and structural complexity were also significant predictors, increasing model explanatory power to 91%. Larger and more heterogeneous particle assemblages were associated with lower microbial carbon turnover, while increased structural complexity was associated with lower turnover after accounting for particle size. Together these findings indicate that particle traits provide additional controls on microbial carbon turnover beyond environmental variables alone.

title: Cross-level correlation and temporal dynamics of hierarchical habitat selection
content: Habitat selection is a fundamentally hierarchical process implying that choices made by animals at broad spatial scales constrain those made at finer ones. How selection for the same habitats relates across hierarchical orders remains largely untested empirically. We investigated whether selection for a given habitat at the larger scale reinforces itself, is independent of, or opposes selection for the same habitat at the finer scale. Using GPS-collared European hares (Lepus europaeus, n = 52) in a mid-mountain grassland landscape (French Jura, 2021-2023), we jointly quantified and compared temporal variation in second-order (home range placement within the landscape) and third-order (habitat use within home ranges) selection with generalised linear mixed models, and resource selection functions. The association in selection strength between orders was strongly habitat-dependent: significantly positive for grasslands, forests and farm tracks, but negative for fodder crops. Our results suggest that hierarchical levels of habitat selection can couple or decouple depending on the habitat considered and what resources European hares are seeking at the different scales. Temporal variability in selection was consistently greater within home ranges than at the landscape level, and seasonal variation in ecological conditions (temperature, precipitation) shaped fine-scale selection while leaving landscape-level selection largely unaffected. Large-scale selection by European hare appeared relatively stable over time while fine-scale selection allowed dynamic behavioural adjustments to short-term variability of environmental conditions. Our results illustrate a hierarchical strategy of stable placement of the home range, flexible use within it. Reliance on heterogeneous open and semi-open habitats and consistent avoidance of built-up areas also clarifies the habitat requirements of the European hare in grassland-dominated agricultural landscapes, given population declines across much of its native range.

title: Taxonomic turnover with phylogenetic conservation in subaerial biofilm (SAB) communities of marble monuments
content: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) colonizing exposed stone surfaces provide natural systems for investigating microbial community assembly under challenging environmental conditions. Although bacterial diversity on stone has been widely described, whether taxonomic variation reflects broader phylogenetic and ecological differences remains unclear. Here, we characterized SAB communities inhabiting two geographically separated historic urban marble monuments, Federal Hall National Memorial (New York) and the Lincoln Memorial (Washington, DC), using SSU rRNA amplicon sequencing. Additional samples from the Merchants' Exchange Building (Philadelphia) were also examined. Bacterial communities exhibited pronounced taxonomic turnover but substantially greater phylogenetic similarity, indicating that community variation primarily reflected replacement among closely related bacterial lineages rather than turnover among distantly related clades. Despite this taxonomic turnover, core assemblage analyses identified conserved bacterial lineages shared across monuments, several of which were also detected in the independent Philadelphia samples. Consistent with these patterns, inferred ecological composition remained remarkably similar among monuments, with chlorophyll-containing bacteria dominating all communities. Together, these findings demonstrate that these monuments harbor distinct bacterial assemblages while maintaining a conserved phylogenetic and inferred ecological framework, suggesting that environmental filtering and local ecological processes may contribute to SAB community assembly across spatial scales.

title: Ecology of Chagas disease vector Triatoma sanguisuga in Delaware: distribution, habitat, host use and Trypanosoma cruzi infection
content: Chagas disease is a vector-borne disease caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by triatomine bugs. The disease is increasingly recognized as an emerging public health threat in the United States (US). Little is known about the Chagas disease system in the Mid-Atlantic US despite the presence of a native T. cruzi vector species, Triatoma sanguisuga. The species is widespread throughout the eastern US, and the Mid-Atlantic comprises the northernmost portion of its geographic range. Triatoma sanguisuga has been implicated in autochthonous T. cruzi transmission to humans in other parts of the US but has never been formally studied in the Mid-Atlantic. To fill this knowledge gap and increase public health preparedness, we investigated T. sanguisuga in Delaware and eastern Maryland. We aimed to collect baseline information about the species, including its habitat, feeding patterns, and T. cruzi infection rates across land use intensities. We collected 151 T. sanguisuga specimens in all three DE counties and two counties in MD, and identified standing dead trees as an important local habitat for the species. Twenty specimens (13.2%) were submitted by community members who had found the bugs in or around human homes and businesses. We detected T. cruzi infection in 23 of 150 (15.3%) specimens and identified 24 vertebrate host species, including humans, from 95 specimens. We detected a stage-structured blood feeding pattern wherein juvenile bugs ("nymphs") were reptile-associated (which are refractory T. cruzi hosts)and adult bugs were mammal-associated (which are competent T. cruzi hosts), which was reflected in a significant difference in T. cruzi infection prevalence between adults and nymphs. Our findings reveal the multiscale network that sustains T. cruzi transmission in Delaware while also providing practical public health information on a local vector-borne disease system.
